title: Operator trigonometric functions
subtitle: G2 lecture 041000 · expanded companion
adaptation: Individually authored from the spoken lecture and its display-only mathematical appendix. Includes stepwise constructions, explicit hypotheses, worked examples and topic-specific vector figures; all slide prose is independent of audio.

slides.title: Trig functions of an operator
slides.lead: For a finite-dimensional self-adjoint A, define sin A and cos A by applying scalar trigonometry to its eigenvalues.
body: The spectral theorem expresses A through mutually orthogonal eigenspace projections. Trigonometric functions reuse those projections and change only the scalar multiplier on each eigenspace.
This construction produces operators that commute with A and with each other, and it preserves familiar trigonometric identities because the calculation reduces to each spectral value.
slides.takeaway: Operator trigonometry is spectral calculus with the scalar functions sine and cosine.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 041000 · Trig functions of an operator

slides.title: The spectral formulas
slides.lead: Keep the same eigenspaces and replace each eigenvalue λ by sin λ or cos λ.
body: For a finite spectral decomposition A=ΣλPλ, both functions are self-adjoint: their coefficients are real and the projectors are self-adjoint.
There is no need to choose particular eigenvectors when eigenvalues repeat. The projection formula is independent of all basis choices within each eigenspace.
slides.takeaway: The trigonometric operators are intrinsic to the spectral decomposition.

slides.title: The power-series construction agrees
slides.lead: Entire scalar functions can also be evaluated by norm-convergent matrix power series.
body: The sine series collects odd powers of A and the cosine series collects even powers. Because both series converge absolutely in finite dimensions, they are valid definitions for any square matrix.
For self-adjoint A, substituting an eigenvector into these series reduces them to the scalar series, confirming the spectral formulas.
slides.takeaway: Spectral calculus and power-series calculus agree for sin and cos.

slides.title: The operator Pythagorean identity
slides.lead: The scalar identity sin²t+cos²t=1 survives evaluation at A.
body: Since the spectral projections are orthogonal idempotents, squares of sin A and cos A act on each λ-eigenspace by sin²λ and cos²λ.
Adding them produces the identity on each eigenspace, hence on the whole space. The operators commute because both are functions of the same self-adjoint A.
slides.takeaway: The familiar trig identity becomes a genuine operator identity.

slides.title: A diagonal worked example
slides.lead: Take A=diag(0,π/3). The two eigendirections undergo different scalar transformations.
body: On the first coordinate the sine vanishes and cosine equals one. On the second, sine equals √3/2 and cosine equals 1/2.
Squaring and adding the two matrices gives I. The example illustrates why we apply the functions to spectral values rather than to the matrix entries without diagonalization.
slides.takeaway: Different spectral directions can carry different angles simultaneously.

slides.title: Why inverse trigonometric functions need a range
slides.lead: Sine and cosine repeat values, so their inverses are not globally single-valued.
body: For a positive angle operator Θ with spectrum in [0,π/2], cosine decreases from 1 to 0 and sine increases from 0 to 1. Both are one-to-one on this interval.
Consequently one can recover Θ from cos Θ or sin Θ using the corresponding inverse function on that restricted spectrum. The spectral interval is an essential hypothesis.
slides.takeaway: Inverse trigonometric operator functions require a specified spectral branch.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 041000 · Why inverse trigonometric functions need a range

slides.title: The block-rotation construction
slides.lead: A self-adjoint Θ defines a length-preserving motion on two copies of the same space.
body: Put cos Θ and sin Θ into the familiar two-by-two rotation pattern, now with operator entries. The entries commute because both are functions of Θ.
Multiplying the block matrix by its adjoint reduces to sin²Θ+cos²Θ=I and cancellation of the mixed terms. The result is a unitary block operator.
slides.takeaway: Functional calculus turns scalar rotation formulas into compatible operator blocks.

slides.title: The principal-angle interpretation
slides.lead: For two subspaces, principal angles are encoded by an angle operator with spectrum in [0,π/2].
body: Its cosine and sine record paired overlap and perpendicular escape. Squaring and adding returns the identity on the coordinate space because every unit direction splits orthogonally into a component inside the target and a component outside it.
The spectral interval makes the angles intrinsic: an angle with cosine c in [0,1] has the single value arccos c in [0,π/2].
slides.takeaway: The angle-operator branch ties operator trig to subspace geometry.

slides.title: Addition formulas require commuting operators
slides.lead: Scalar addition formulas generalize to operator arguments when the operators commute.
body: Suppose A and B are commuting self-adjoint matrices. They admit a common orthonormal eigenbasis, so evaluating sine and cosine on A+B reduces to the scalar angle-addition formulas on each shared eigenspace.

Without commutation, the products sin A cos B and cos B sin A may differ, and there is no reason for the scalar identities to extend in the same form. The hypothesis matters even though each function is individually well-defined.
slides.takeaway: Commuting spectral calculi inherit familiar scalar identities.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 041000 · Addition formulas require commuting operators

slides.title: Recover the identities
slides.lead: Begin with a diagonal self-adjoint A and verify each statement eigenvalue by eigenvalue.
body: Then use the projector formula to show that the result does not depend on a diagonalizing basis. Derive the block-rotation identity explicitly from commutation and the operator Pythagorean identity.
Finally explain why arccos cos Θ identifies Θ only when the spectrum is restricted to a range where cosine is injective.
slides.takeaway: Spectral selection and functional calculus make operator trigonometry rigorous.
